# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/main/src/CDPVault.sol#L702
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/main/src/PoolV3.sol#L593


# Vulnerability details

## Description

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi-findings/issues/57 showed a scenario where the profit from the interest is not being registered correctly. It shows a mitigation that consists of 2 parts, but only 1 was implemented which reversed the issue and made it more severe.

The mitigation that was added was `pool.repayCreditAccount(debtData.debt, profit, loss);`, `profit` was set to 0 before the mitigation. 

## Proof of Concept
From the original report:
>First we need to understand how liquidatePositionBadDebt() works. When there is a bad debt detected for a position, any liquidator can come and liquidate the position. The liquidator is required to buy ALL the collateral at a discount price, and the loss (totalDebt - repayAmount) is sent to PoolV3 to be beared by the lpETH stakers.
>
>This is all good, but the issue here is that when the liquidator repays the debt, it is compared against the totalDebt of the position, which includes the interest. This interest should also be sent to the lpETH stakers, but is currently not, which would result in loss of funds for the lpETH stakers.
>
>An example:
>1. CDPVault position has debt principal == 1000, debt interest == 500. Total debt == 1500. Collateral value == 1600, discount == 90%, discount value == 1440.
>2. Liquidator comes and pay off 1440, loss is 1500-1440 = 60, so pool.repayCreditAccount(1000, 0, 60) is called.
>3. The loss is 60, and the same amount of lpETH is burned from the StakingLPEth contract.

Here comes the reversed impact, where with the current implementation only the profit will be registered because of `PoolV3::repayCreditAccount:
```solidity
if (profit > 0) {
    _mint(treasury, _convertToShares(profit)); // U:[LP-14B]
} else if (loss > 0) {
    ...
    _burn(treasury_, sharesToBurn); // U:[LP-14C,14D]
}
```
Where only the profit part will run, and the "else if" part is thrown away. This means that the loss amount that happened (60) won't be registered and the treasury shares won't be burned, messing up the assets/shares ratio, which affects all `lpETH` stakers forcing their shares to be worth fewer assets, i.e. losing funds.


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

In `PoolV3::repayCreditAccount`:
```diff
        if (profit > 0) {
            _mint(treasury, convertToShares(profit)); // U:[LP-14B]
+       }
+       if (loss > 0)
-       } else if (loss > 0) {
            ...
        }
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The uninitialized mapping access in the RewardManagerAbstract contract can lead to incorrect reward calculations, allowing attackers to exploit the reward distribution system. When a user who has never received rewards before interacts with the system, the default values of the userReward mapping will result in unintended behavior:

1. Unauthorized Reward Accrual: An attacker can manipulate their interaction with the contract to receive rewards without a valid stake or contribution.
2. Financial Loss: Honest users may find their rewards diluted or incorrect, leading to potential financial losses due to erroneous distributions.

## Proof of Concept
https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/d219f0132005b00a68f505edc22b34f9a8b49766/src/pendle-rewards/RewardManagerAbstract.sol#L65-L65

Here is how an attacker can exploit this vulnerability;

1. Setup:

An attacker deploys a contract that interacts with the vulnerable RewardManagerAbstract.
They ensure that their address has never received rewards before.

2. Triggering the Vulnerability:

The attacker calls a function that leads to [_distributeRewardsPrivate](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/d219f0132005b00a68f505edc22b34f9a8b49766/src/pendle-rewards/RewardManagerAbstract.sol#L52C5-L79C6) being executed.
In _distributeRewardsPrivate, the following line is executed:
```solidity
uint256 userIndex = userReward[token][user].index; // Returns 0 for uninitialized mapping
```
3. Exploit Mechanics:

Since userIndex is 0, the following calculations in the function will proceed incorrectly:
```solidity
uint256 deltaIndex = index - userIndex; // If index > 0, deltaIndex > 0
```

This results in a positive deltaIndex, allowing the attacker to calculate rewardDelta based on a non-zero delta:
```solidity
uint256 rewardDelta = userShares.mulDown(deltaIndex);
```

4. Outcome:

The attacker receives rewardDelta without having contributed any collateral or having any prior reward accumulation.
This could lead to the attacker accruing significant rewards simply by exploiting the mapping's default behavior.

## Tools Used
Vscode, Manual Analysis

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

1. Initialize Mappings: Ensure that when a user first interacts with the reward system, their mapping entry is initialized with default values:

```solidity
userReward[token][user] = UserReward({index: INITIAL_REWARD_INDEX.Uint128(), accrued: 0});
```

2. Use Require Statements: Before accessing user reward mappings, implement checks to ensure users have valid entries:

```solidity
require(userReward[token][user].index != 0, "User not initialized");
```

# Vulnerability details

```solidity
function moveFunds(address treasury, IERC20[] calldata tokens) external onlyRole(FUNDS_ADMINISTRATOR_ROLE) {
    uint256 len = tokens.length;
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        _moveFunds(treasury, tokens[i]);
    }
}
```

## Description:
The `moveFunds` function iterates over an arbitrary number of `ERC20` tokens provided in the tokens array and transfers each token to a new treasury address. If the array contains a large number of tokens, the function could become gas-intensive, potentially exceeding the block's gas limit. As a result, the transaction may fail, making it impossible to move funds when dealing with a significant number of tokens in a single call.

## Impact:
If the tokens array is excessively large, the gas required to complete the transaction will exceed the gas limit, resulting in a failed transaction. This could render the `moveFunds` function unusable for large sets of tokens, effectively causing a denial of service for transferring funds in bulk. The treasury might be left unable to move funds, increasing the risk of operational issues or disruptions.

## Proof of Concept (PoC):
A large number of `ERC20 `tokens (e.g., hundreds or thousands) are passed to `moveFunds`.
The contract loops through each token in the array.
Due to the gas cost of handling so many tokens, the transaction fails, and no funds are moved.

## Tool Used:
Manual Review.

## Recommended Mitigation:
 Introduce a mechanism to process tokens in batches, limiting the number of tokens transferred in a single transaction to avoid exceeding the gas limit.
 Refactor the loop to optimize gas consumption, for instance, by reducing unnecessary operations or combining multiple actions into one where possible.
 Consider moving token list handling off-chain to reduce the amount of on-chain computation required for fund transfers.

# Vulnerability details


## Impact
The current reward distribution mechanism is vulnerable to manipulation, allowing users to artificially inflate their rewards by directly transferring tokens to the vault. This can lead to unfair distribution of rewards, dilution of legitimate rewards, and potential draining of reward tokens from the system. The impact is significant as it undermines the fairness and sustainability of the entire reward system.

## Proof of Concept
The vulnerability exists in the [`_updateRewardIndex`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/main/src/pendle-rewards/RewardManager.sol#L44) function of the `RewardManager` contract:

```Solidity
function _updateRewardIndex()
    internal
    virtual
    override
    returns (address[] memory tokens, uint256[] memory indexes)
{
    // ... [previous code]

    for (uint256 i = 0; i < tokens.length; ++i) {
        address token = tokens[i];

        RewardState memory _state = rewardState[token];
        (uint256 lastBalance, uint256 index) = (_state.lastBalance, _state.index);

        uint256 accrued = IERC20(tokens[i]).balanceOf(vault) - lastBalance;

        // ... [rest of the function]
    }
}
```

The issue arises from the calculation of `accrued` rewards. It assumes that any increase in the vault's token balance is due to legitimate rewards. However, this assumption can be exploited:
- An attacker observes the current balance of a reward token in the vault.
- The attacker transfers additional tokens directly to the vault address.
- When `_updateRewardIndex` is next called, the `accrued` value will include the attacker's transferred tokens.
- This inflated `accrued` value increases the reward index, benefiting the attacker unfairly.

This issue allows an attacker to increase their share of rewards without actually contributing to the protocol.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Implement a tracking mechanism for rewards that doesn't rely on balance differences. Instead of using the vault's token balance, maintain a separate accounting system for rewards. This could involve:
. Directly tracking the amount of rewards received from `market.redeemRewards(address(vault))`.
. Updating a dedicated rewards accumulator instead of relying on token balances.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/main/src/PoolV3.sol#L694


# Vulnerability details

### **Summary**:
A front-running vulnerability exists in the `_updateBaseInterest()` function due to the improper reliance on `block.timestamp` for determining when to update the `lastBaseInterestUpdate` variable. An attacker can exploit this by calling the function just before the victim, preventing the victim’s transaction from executing the interest update logic.


### **Affected Function**: PoolV3.sol#L694

```solidity
function _updateBaseInterest(
  ...
) internal {
   ...
    uint256 lastBaseInterestUpdate_ = lastBaseInterestUpdate;
 ->   if (block.timestamp != lastBaseInterestUpdate_) {  // @audit-issue  Front-running
        _baseInterestIndexLU = _calcBaseInterestIndex(lastBaseInterestUpdate_).toUint128();
        lastBaseInterestUpdate = uint40(block.timestamp);
    }

   ...
}
```

### **Description**:

* The function relies on the condition `if (block.timestamp != lastBaseInterestUpdate_)` to determine whether to update the base interest. However, because `block.timestamp` remains the same within the same block, an attacker can front-run the victim's transaction by calling the function in the same block. This will update the `lastBaseInterestUpdate` to the current `block.timestamp`.

* As a result, when the victim’s transaction is processed within the same block, the condition `block.timestamp != lastBaseInterestUpdate_` will be `false`, and the interest update logic will be skipped, causing a failure to correctly update the base interest for the victim.

### **Steps to Reproduce**:
1. Attacker monitors for when a victim is about to call the `_updateBaseInterest()` function.
2. Attacker sends a transaction calling `_updateBaseInterest()` just before the victim's transaction is mined.
3. The attacker's transaction updates `lastBaseInterestUpdate` to the current `block.timestamp`.
4. The victim’s transaction is mined within the same block, but the `block.timestamp != lastBaseInterestUpdate_` condition fails.

To prevent slippage-related losses, it is recommended to introduce a slippage protection mechanism within the `withdraw` and `redeem` functions. This would allow users to set a slippage tolerance, ensuring that if the conversion rate changes by more than a specified percentage, the transaction is reverted.

- Allowing users to specify the **minimum number of assets** they expect to receive when calling `withdraw`.
- Allowing users to specify the **maximum number of shares** they are willing to redeem for a specific amount of assets.

By incorporating slippage control parameters, users will have greater protection against adverse changes in the vault's exchange rate, reducing the risk of unexpected fund losses.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/d219f0132005b00a68f505edc22b34f9a8b49766/src/pendle-rewards/RewardManager.sol#L74

# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
Rewards might be lost due to the error that _updateRewardIndex() might advance ```lastBalance``` without advancing index for a reward token. 

Analysis: 
The function ```_updateRewardIndex()``` is used to update the ```lastBalance``` and ```index``` of each reward  token. This function will be called when a user deposit, withdraw collateral or claim rewards. 

However, the function might not advance ```index``` when ```accrued.divDown(totalShares) = 0```, this might happen when ```totalShares``` is too big, and ```accrued``` is too small. One case is that the number of decimals for the reward token is too small.

[https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/d219f0132005b00a68f505edc22b34f9a8b49766/src/pendle-rewards/RewardManager.sol#L74](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/d219f0132005b00a68f505edc22b34f9a8b49766/src/pendle-rewards/RewardManager.sol#L74)

For example, the USDC token only has 6 decimals. 

Suppose ```accrued``` = $100 = 100*10**6, and ```totalShares``` = 200M = 200 * 10** 6 * 10**18, 
then we have  ```accrued.divDown(totalShares) = 0```. 

Furthermore, if function ```_updateRewardIndex()``` is called more frequently, either because a malicious user keeps calling ```getRewards()```  (the gas fee is low on Arbitrum) or simply because the community is large so there is a high chance that for each block (per 12 seconds on Ethereum), there is someone who calls a withdraw/deposit/getRewards function. As a result,  ```accrued``` could be small, leading to ```accrued.divDown(totalShares) = 0```.

Meanwhile, ```_updateRewardIndex()``` always advance ```lastBalance``` when ```accrued !=0 ```:

[https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/d219f0132005b00a68f505edc22b34f9a8b49766/src/pendle-rewards/RewardManager.sol#L78](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-loopfi/blob/d219f0132005b00a68f505edc22b34f9a8b49766/src/pendle-rewards/RewardManager.sol#L78)

This means the accrued rewards are lost! Nobody will receive the rewards since index has not changed. 

More importantly, due to the rounding down error for ```accrued.divDown(totalShares)```, there is always a slight loss for the rewards, which is accumulative over time.  


The following mitigation will fix this problem. 


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The fix is simple: 
calculate ```deltaIndex = accrued.divDown(totalShares)```, and advance ```lastBalance``` by ```deltaIndex.mulDown(totalShares)```. In this way, ```index``` and ```lastBalance``` will always advance in the same pace, in particular if index does not advance, then ```lastBalance``` will not advance either. The rounding down error is eliminated too since the ```lastBalance``` will not by ```accrued``` but by ```deltaIndex.mulDown(totalShares)```~~~

Math
